title: Easily confused words
subtitle: intervene / interfere, shade / shadow, outrun / run out
summary: Choose correctly between pairs that look or feel alike - intervene and interfere, continually and continuously, shade and shadow - and between verbs whose particle comes first or second.

left.label: intervene
left.text: Step in. Neutral in meaning - often the right thing to do.
examples: The United Nations should **intervene** to stop the civil war.
The teacher **intervened** to stop the argument between the two students.

right.label: interfere
right.text: Involve yourself where you are not wanted. Negative and critical.
examples: She shouldn't **interfere** in things that don't concern her.
I have always tried not to **interfere** in things that are not my business.

left.label: continually
left.text: Very frequently, again and again. Often negative - it suggests annoyance.
examples: The phone's been ringing **continually**. It's driving me crazy.
He was **continually** complaining about something or other.

right.label: continuously
examples: Stir the mixture **continuously** until it boils.
You have to press the button **continuously** until the green light comes on.

lesson.heading: More pairs that are close in meaning
lesson.text: A **series** is a set of related programmes; a **serial** is a set of programmes where the story continues across the episodes. You sit in the **shade** of a tree (out of the sun, a pleasant word), but the sun casts **shadows** - dark areas or shapes - and living **in the shadow of** something means being dominated by it, which is negative.

examples.text: There's a new **series** on TV about space exploration.
I don't want to miss this week's episode of Oliver Twist. It's a **serial** - if I miss one, I'll lose track of the story.
He was dozing happily in the **shade** of an old beech tree.
The moon sometimes casts wonderful **shadows** on the sea.
They lived **in the shadow of** a chemical factory.

left.label: compliment
left.text: Praise someone, express admiration for them.
examples: She **complimented** me on my performance at the concert.

right.label: complement
right.text: Make something seem better, more complete or more attractive in combination.
examples: I took a course in programming to **complement** my other IT skills.

lesson.heading: Different words, same area of meaning
rows: moist
slightly wet - often in recipes, a good thing
The cake mixture should be **moist** but not sticky.
damp
slightly wet in an unpleasant way
The climate in the north is **damp** and rather cold.
theme
the main idea that everything follows
The **theme** of the festival was '1,000 years of culture'.
topic
what people happen to be talking about
The **topic** of conversation soon changed to the news.
security
protection of property and people from crime
The **security** officer noticed a broken window.
safety
prevention of accidents
The **safety** officer told him that he must wear a helmet.
avoid
stay away from
We took a smaller road in order to **avoid** the roadworks.
evade
escape from - more formal
The escaped prisoner **evaded** capture for three months.

lesson.heading: Phrasal verbs and their noun forms
rows: Six men **broke out** of the prison.
There was a **breakout** at the prison.
The disease has **broken out** in several villages.
There has been an **outbreak** of the disease in several villages.
Economists are **looking out for** signs of recovery.
The **outlook** is not good - the economy seems stagnant.
He stood at the corner, **looking out for** police cars.
He was the **lookout** while the others robbed the bank.
The club decided to **set up** a committee.
The company **setup** is quite complex, with branches in 30 countries.
lesson.note: A stomach **upset** is the noun from upset - a mild illness that stops you eating or working normally.

lesson.heading: Particle first or particle second?
rows: **upend** = move into a vertical position
**end up** = finish, eventually be somewhere
**uphold** = confirm, support
**hold up** = delay
**outdo** = do better than
**do out** = decorate
**outrun** = run faster than
**run out** = use something so there is none left
**upset** = make someone worried, unhappy or angry
**set up** = organise or arrange something
lesson.note: Common prepositions often act as prefixes: over (overcook, overcome), in (input, income).

lesson.text: Security guards worry about thieves; safety officers worry about accidents.

exercises.prompt: I have always tried not to ___ in things that are not my business.
exercises.explanation: Interfere is negative and critical - involving yourself where you are not wanted.

exercises.prompt: ___ at the factory is not good. There have been several accidents involving machinery recently.
exercises.explanation: Safety is about the prevention of accidents; security is about protection from crime.

exercises.prompt: There are some ___ I don't like to talk about with my friends, such as politics and religion.
exercises.explanation: A topic is what people talk about; a theme is the main idea running through something.

exercises.prompt: He was dozing happily in the ___ of an old beech tree.
exercises.explanation: Shade means out of the sun and has a pleasant connotation.

exercises.prompt: The ___ of her latest novel is growing up as an only child in the 1970s.
exercises.explanation: The theme is the main idea that everything in the novel follows.

exercises.prompt: The teacher ___ to stop the argument between the two students.
exercises.explanation: Intervene is neutral - to step in. Interfere would criticise the teacher.

exercises.prompt: The receptionist called the ___ officer once it became clear that there had been a burglary.
exercises.explanation: Security is concerned with the protection of property from crime.

exercises.prompt: He was ___ complaining about something or other.
exercises.explanation: Continually means very frequently and is often negative; continuously means without stopping.

exercises.prompt: The moon sometimes casts wonderful ___ on the sea.
exercises.explanation: Shadows are the dark areas or shapes cast by light; shade is the pleasant place out of the sun.

exercises.prompt: You have to press the button ___ until the green light comes on. Don't take your finger off it.
exercises.explanation: Continuously means without stopping at all.

exercises.prompt: The cheetah is so fast it can ___ a fast-moving vehicle.
exercises.explanation: Outrun means run faster than; run out means use something until there is none left.

exercises.prompt: The police ___ the traffic while the President's car passed.
exercises.explanation: Hold up means delay; uphold means confirm or support.

exercises.prompt: Sean made an insensitive comment and didn't realise how much he'd ___ Wendy.
exercises.explanation: Upset means make someone worried, unhappy or angry; set up means organise or arrange.

exercises.prompt: The committee ___ her complaint, and she was awarded compensation.
exercises.explanation: Uphold means confirm or support a decision or complaint.

exercises.prompt: We decided to ___ the living room and went online to choose paint colours.
exercises.explanation: Do out means decorate; outdo means do better than someone.

exercises.prompt: We ___ the sofa and used it to block the doorway.
exercises.hint: (set/end + up - move into a vertical position)
exercises.explanation: Upend means move something into a vertical position; end up means finish.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with the noun that fits it.

pairs.left: There has been violence in the capital city.
My stomach was bad so I couldn't go to work.
The prospects for the economy are good over the coming years.
I wanted to learn more about how the business was organised.
She made sure nobody was looking while her husband stole.
Four prisoners have escaped from a maximum security prison.

exercises.prompt: Which word of each pair would you expect in a recipe, and which in a weather report?

exercises.statement: If you complement someone, you tell them how much you admire them.
exercises.explanation: That is compliment. To complement something is to make it more complete or attractive in combination.

exercises.answer: The escaped prisoner evaded capture for three months
exercises.explanation: Evade is the more formal word for escaping from something; avoid simply means stay away from.
